sentences.text: Solicitor Daniel Okafor and trainee Sophie Grant attended the meeting on Wednesday, 23 September 2026. The purpose was for the solicitor to gather the client's account of events and establish the facts surrounding her dismissal from Northgate Logistics.
The trainee Sophie Grant was present to take copies of documents the client had brought and to assist with the preparation of the subject access request.

The client, Aisha Rahman, started working at Northgate Logistics Limited on 5 March 2018, in a picker role, and was promoted to team leader of the inbound goods team in June 2021. She held the team leader position for eight and a half years until her dismissal on 14 August 2026.

Her basic annual salary was £29,400, with a shift allowance of approximately £1,800 per year, which she described as 'unsocial hours supplement'. She did not know the exact pension contribution, but believed it was around 5%.

The client has type one diabetes, which she has had since age 14. She manages it with a glucose sensor on her arm, which sends data to her phone app, and requires regular checks and glucose tablets or juice when her levels drop. She described that it is not possible to schedule these checks and that

The client informed Northgate of her diabetes when she started work and provided the information on the health form. Her manager, Linda Chu, was supportive and allowed her to step off the dock for short breaks when needed, without written policy or formal arrangements. Linda left the company at the

After Linda's departure, Gary Whitlock became the operations manager for the inbound team and started in January 2026. In February 2026, he sent an email requiring all staff to take breaks at fixed times and to leave the dock only with his permission. The client did not have a copy of this email.

The client discussed her diabetes with Gary in February 2026 and asked him to allow her to step off for short breaks when needed. He responded that she should time her breaks with the scheduled ones. She later emailed HR in March 2026 to request an occupational health referral, which was granted on

The occupational health report, dated 22 April 2026, stated that the client should be allowed short breaks to test and eat as a 'reasonable adjustment'. The client believes this report was sent to her personal email and is currently searching for it.

In May 2026, Gary had the client in a 'conversation' on 19 May, where he said her team were seeing her leave the dock and that she needed to set an example as a team leader. The client was not given a warning, letter, or formal notice, and no written record of this meeting exists.

On 1 July 2026, the client experienced two low glucose episodes and stepped off the dock twice, each time telling Tomasz to cover. On 3 July, she stepped off again. On 9 July, due to high heat, she experienced a low reading, became confused, and sat on a pallet. Marcus Bell, a first aider, provided

On 9 July, the client was unable to stand and could not hold a radio, and was told by Gary to go home. She lost approximately four and a half hours of work and was not paid for this time. No accident form or first aid log was provided by Gary, though Marcus filled in the first aid log.

The client has provided the following documents: the dismissal letter (dated 14 August 2026), the appeal outcome letter (dated 16 September 2026), her original 2018 employment contract, and payslips for May, June, July, and August 2026.

The client does not have a copy of the February 2026 email from Gary about fixed breaks, nor the notes from the investigation meeting on 17 July 2026 or the disciplinary meeting on 6 August 2026. She also does not have a copy of the occupational health report, which she believes was sent to her via
The client has a photo of her glucose sensor taken by Marcus Bell on 9 July 2026, with the timestamp 14:06. This photo is stored in her WhatsApp chat with Marcus.
The client has not received any settlement agreement, offer letter, or document from Northgate since the appeal outcome on 16 September 2026.
The client's primary objective is for Northgate to acknowledge that their handling of her case was incorrect, particularly in relation to her diabetes and the failure to make reasonable adjustments.
The client wants a proper reference to be provided so she can secure future employment, as she is concerned that any new employer will be told she was dismissed by Northgate.
Compensation is secondary to the above, though she acknowledged it would be helpful if the claim were successful.
The client expressed a desire for Northgate to ensure that any similar employees with medical conditions, such as a colleague with epilepsy, are supported with reasonable adjustments.

The solicitor advised that the client has more than two years of service, so she can bring an unfair dismissal claim, and that type one diabetes is likely to be considered a disability under the Equality Act 2010.

The solicitor advised that the claims are likely to be unfair dismissal and discrimination arising from disability, due to the dismissal being linked to her diabetes and failure to make reasonable adjustments, especially given the occupational health report.

The solicitor highlighted procedural concerns, including Gary chairing the disciplinary hearing as the person who originally raised the issue, the absence of any prior warnings, the failure to provide meeting notes, and the dismissal letter not mentioning her diabetes or the OH report.

The solicitor advised that the client must notify ACAS for early conciliation within three months less one day of the effective date of dismissal, which is 14 August 2026, so the deadline is 13 November 2026. The solicitor recommended notifying ACAS by the 16 October 2026 to allow sufficient time.

The solicitor advised that the client should not sign any settlement agreement or dismissal letter without first consulting the solicitor, and that she should not respond to any correspondence from Northgate directly.

The solicitor advised that the client should contact Castleford Mutual to check if her home insurance policy includes legal expenses cover, and if so, to provide the policy wording and schedule for review.
The solicitor advised that a reference could be negotiated as part of a settlement through ACAS, and that this would be the most important outcome for the client.
By Friday 25 September 2026, the client must email the solicitor the occupational health report, Marcus's photo of the sensor, and any additional payslips she has not already provided.
By Monday 28 September 2026, the client must check with Castleford Mutual whether her policy includes legal expenses cover and send the policy schedule and wording to the solicitor.
By Friday 2 October 2026, the client must provide a timeline in her own words, including all key dates from the meeting, as best she can, with bullet points if needed.
The trainee Sophie Grant will draft a subject access request to Northgate by Monday 29 September 2026, which will be sent to both the HR inbox and the company's registered office.
The solicitor will send a letter confirming today's advice, including the time limits (with the 13 November 2026 deadline in bold), by Tuesday 29 September 2026.

The client is to ask Marcus Bell whether he would be willing to provide a statement, without going into detail. Tomasz is to be approached only if the client feels comfortable doing so, and Linda Chu is to be contacted to see if she would be willing to speak at a later date.
The next meeting is scheduled for Thursday 8 October 2026 at 10:00, where the client will provide the documents and the insurance check, and the team will aim to notify ACAS by 16 October 2026.
If Northgate sends any letter, offer, or document to the client, it must be sent to the solicitor before the client responds.
